content.text: {"conditions":{"rc1":{"status":"review","note":"The pecuniary denial can be traced to the stated absence of receipts, bills, and loan documentation, but the $25,000 non-pecuniary base figure cannot be reconstructed: the record says only that 'the case law supports' it, while also finding 'no plausible evidence' of any long-term condition."},"rc2":{"status":"review","note":"Most characterizations are tied to identified sources (Complainant's affidavit, statements from his wife, sister and mother, and the 'Note From Hawaii Pacific Health'), but the case law behind the $25,000 figure is not cited and the documents for the 'three medical visits' are not identified when only two visits are described."},"rc3":{"status":"review","note":"Key dates are present (June–December 2020 period, December 30, 2020 complaint, August 17, 2021 decision, August 17, 2023 EEOC decision, October 10, 2023 report), but the compensatory-damages final decision is undated, the AWOL date is given only as October 2020, and the account of treatment conflicts (psychiatrist call December 1, 2020 versus 'first sought psychological counseling on December 21, 2020')."},"rc4":{"status":"review","note":"The applicable standards are stated (causation, exacerbation of pre-existing conditions, no recovery for EEO-process distress, no punitive damages) and Complainant's and witnesses' submissions were weighed, but the decision is attributed only to 'the Agency' with no identified reviewer or decision-maker."},"rc5":{"status":"review","note":"The record largely stands on its own for the pecuniary denial, but an independent reviewer cannot fully evaluate the $26,500 award without the uncited comparative case law, the missing final-decision date, and resolution of the inconsistent treatment dates and visit count."}}}
